planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a fast spring crop, or in midsummer for fall; Green Comet was one of the earliest hybrid broccolis widely sold and remains valued for reaching harvest well before slower open-pollinated types.

directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting transplants into fertile, evenly moist soil, spacing plants closer than later-maturing types since this hybrid stays compact. Green Comet earned an All-America Selections award for its speed, forming a tight, uniformly domed blue-green head only about eight weeks after transplanting, which makes it a reliable choice for short-season gardens or an early jump on the spring harvest before summer heat arrives. Side shoots follow the main head, though they are smaller and less numerous than in later hybrids. Cut the central head promptly once buds are tight, since this variety runs to flower quickly in warm weather.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring, or in midsummer for fall; Gypsy is bred to tolerate the heat and stress of summer plantings better than most broccoli, so it fills the gap between spring and fall crops.

directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist soil. Gypsy is a widely grown hybrid selected for adaptability across a broad sowing window, holding quality through the heat and inconsistent weather of a summer planting better than many broccoli varieties, which makes it a dependable choice for closing the gap between an early spring crop and a fall one. It forms medium-large, tightly beaded blue-green heads and continues producing a generous flush of side shoots after the main head is harvested. Cut the central head while the buds are firm and tightly closed, then keep picking side shoots as they reach the same stage.

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost for a fall harvest; Churchill is a vigorous, reliable mid-season hybrid favored by market growers for its heavy, even sprout set.

directions: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before the first fall frost and transplant into firm, fertile, well-drained soil; stake tall plants to keep them upright as sprouts fill in. Churchill is a dependable mid-season Brussels sprout hybrid known for setting a heavy, closely spaced column of smooth, dark green sprouts along a sturdy stalk, and for standing well in the garden without the stems toppling or the sprouts loosening. Its moderate cold tolerance lets it carry a harvest through the first hard frosts, which sweetens the sprouts. Pick from the bottom of the stalk upward once sprouts firm to about an inch across, and remove yellowing lower leaves as you go to improve air circulation.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring, or in midsummer for a fall crop; Fremont's leaves naturally wrap over the developing curd, so it needs little to no manual blanching.

directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil. Fremont is a self-blanching hybrid whose upright inner leaves curl naturally over the forming curd, shielding it from sunlight and keeping the head bright white without the usual step of tying leaves up by hand. It performs reliably through the warmer, less predictable conditions of a summer planting, forming smooth, dense, well-domed heads. Harvest as soon as the curd is tight and fully formed, since cauliflower heads can quickly become ricey or loose if left too long once mature.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Premium Late Flat Dutch'

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost for spring planting, or in early summer for a fall/winter storage crop; this improved strain of the old Flat Dutch line needs the full growing season to bulk up its heads.

directions: Start indoors and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil, giving plants extra room since this is one of the larger-headed cabbages. Premium Late Flat Dutch is a 19th-century American heirloom line prized for its very large, flattened, blue-green heads that can reach ten pounds or more and hold together tightly rather than splitting. Its long time to maturity and dense, thick leaves make it an excellent late-season crop for slaw, kraut, and cold storage, where whole heads keep for months in a cool root cellar. Because of its size, allow it a full, uninterrupted season of growth and avoid crowding neighboring plants.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, or in early summer for a fall harvest destined for winter storage; this Danish-type cabbage is bred specifically for keeping quality rather than early eating.

directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, timing the crop to mature in the cooler days of fall. Storage No. 4 is a Danish-type cabbage bred above all for keeping quality, forming dense, hard, pale green heads that resist splitting in the field and hold their crispness for months in cold, humid storage such as a root cellar. Its heads are somewhat smaller and firmer than fresh-market types, a trait that directly supports its long shelf life. Harvest before hard freezes settle in and store whole heads with roots trimmed for the longest keeping.
